Let

\[
f(x)=\sqrt[n]{1+x}+\sqrt[n]{1-x}.
\]

We consider the real-valued function \(f\). If \(n\) is even, the domain is \([-1,1]\); if \(n\) is odd, the domain is \(\mathbb R\). In both cases the domain is symmetric about \(0\), and

\[
f(-x)=\sqrt[n]{1-x}+\sqrt[n]{1+x}=f(x),
\]

so \(f\) is an even function.

Therefore, if \(x\) is a real solution, then \(-x\) is also a real solution. Hence, if the equation

\[
f(x)=a
\]

has exactly one real root, that root must be

\[
x=0.
\]

Substituting \(x=0\),

\[
a=f(0)=\sqrt[n]{1}+\sqrt[n]{1}=2.
\]

So \(a=2\) is the only possible candidate.

It remains to check that \(a=2\) indeed gives exactly one real solution.

Let \(p=\frac1n\), so \(0<p<1\). For \(0<x<1\),

\[
f'(x)
=p\left((1+x)^{p-1}-(1-x)^{p-1}\right).
\]

Since \(p-1<0\), the function \(t\mapsto t^{p-1}\) is decreasing for \(t>0\). Because \(1+x>1-x>0\), we have

\[
(1+x)^{p-1}<(1-x)^{p-1},
\]

so

\[
f'(x)<0 \qquad (0<x<1).
\]

Thus \(f\) is strictly decreasing on \([0,1]\), and

\[
f(x)<f(0)=2 \qquad (0<x\le 1).
\]

By evenness, the same holds for \(-1\le x<0\).

If \(n\) is even, the domain is exactly \([-1,1]\), so \(f(x)=2\) has the unique solution \(x=0\).

If \(n\) is odd, we must also consider \(|x|>1\). For \(x>1\), write \(x=1+t\) with \(t>0\). Then

\[
f(x)=(1+x)^p+(1-x)^p=(2+t)^p-t^p.
\]

Its derivative with respect to \(t\) is

\[
p\left((2+t)^{p-1}-t^{p-1}\right)<0,
\]

so

\[
f(x)<f(1)=2^p<2.
\]

By symmetry, the same is true for \(x<-1\). Hence for all \(x\neq 0\),

\[
f(x)<2,
\]

while \(f(0)=2\). Therefore \(a=2\) indeed gives exactly one real root.

Thus the only real value of \(a\) is

\[
\boxed{2}
\]
